NUS ST2334 — Probability & Statistics¶

Methodical, Intuitive, Simulation-First Case Studies with Bokeh¶

This notebook is built for a student seeing probability and statistical inference for the first time.

Every major topic follows the same learning cycle:

[ \boxed{ \text{Intuition} \rightarrow \text{Question} \rightarrow \text{Assumptions} \rightarrow \text{Model} \rightarrow \text{Simulation} \rightarrow \text{Bokeh Visual} \rightarrow \text{Interpretation} } ]

The emphasis is not on memorising formulas. It is on understanding what random quantity is being modelled, why a particular distribution applies, what assumptions are being made, and what repeated sampling would look like.

Main case studies¶

  1. Fraud monitoring — conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
  2. Data-centre reliability — Binomial and Poisson models
  3. API traffic — Geometric/Exponential waiting times
  4. Latency analytics — expectation, variance, dependence
  5. Sampling from skewed populations — Central Limit Theorem and standard error
  6. Confidence intervals — repeated-sampling coverage
  7. A/B testing — hypothesis tests, confidence intervals and power
  8. System optimisation — paired inference

All charts use Bokeh.

In [1]:
# Optional if your environment is missing packages:
# %pip install numpy pandas scipy bokeh

import math
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

from bokeh.io import output_notebook, show
from bokeh.plotting import figure
from bokeh.layouts import row, gridplot
from bokeh.models import ColumnDataSource, HoverTool, Span

output_notebook()

RNG = np.random.default_rng(42)

print("Environment ready.")
Loading BokehJS ... 
Environment ready.

How to study with this notebook¶

For each simulation:

  1. Predict first. What should happen if a parameter increases?
  2. Run the code.
  3. Describe the graph in words.
  4. Explain why it looks that way.
  5. Change exactly one parameter.
  6. Run again and compare.

That habit is more valuable than passively reading formulas.

Part A — Probability¶

Probability moves in the direction

[ \boxed{\text{known model} \rightarrow \text{possible data}} ]

while statistics later reverses this direction:

[ \boxed{\text{observed data} \rightarrow \text{unknown model}} ]

That distinction organizes almost the entire course.

1. Sample spaces, events and counting¶

For a fair die,

[ \Omega={1,2,3,4,5,6} ]

is the sample space.

Let

[ A={\text{even}}={2,4,6} ]

and

[ B={X>3}={4,5,6}. ]

Then

[ A\cap B={4,6},\qquad A\cup B={2,4,5,6}. ]

The addition rule

[ P(A\cup B)¶

P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) ]

subtracts the overlap because otherwise it would be counted twice.

Counting¶

If order matters,

[ P(n,r)=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}. ]

If order does not matter,

[ \binom nr=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}. ]

A useful diagnostic question is:

If I swap two selected objects, do I consider that a different outcome?

In [2]:
omega = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
A = {2, 4, 6}
B = {4, 5, 6}

def event_probability(event, sample_space):
    return len(event) / len(sample_space)

print("P(A) =", event_probability(A, omega))
print("P(B) =", event_probability(B, omega))
print("P(A∩B) =", event_probability(A & B, omega))
print("P(A∪B) =", event_probability(A | B, omega))

n, r = 10, 3
print("Ordered selections:", math.perm(n, r))
print("Unordered selections:", math.comb(n, r))

P(A) = 0.5
P(B) = 0.5
P(A∩B) = 0.3333333333333333
P(A∪B) = 0.6666666666666666
Ordered selections: 720
Unordered selections: 120

Case Study 1 — Fraud alerts and Bayes' theorem¶

The question¶

A fraud detector raises an alert. How likely is the transaction actually fraudulent?

Suppose:

[ P(F)=0.01 ]

[ P(A\mid F)=0.90 ]

[ P(A\mid F^c)=0.05. ]

We want

[ P(F\mid A). ]

A classic mistake is to confuse

[ P(A\mid F) ]

with

[ P(F\mid A). ]

These are different conditional probabilities.

In [3]:
prior_fraud = 0.01
sensitivity = 0.90
false_positive_rate = 0.05

p_alert = (
    sensitivity * prior_fraud
    + false_positive_rate * (1 - prior_fraud)
)

posterior_fraud = (
    sensitivity * prior_fraud / p_alert
)

print(f"P(Alert) = {p_alert:.4f}")
print(f"P(Fraud | Alert) = {posterior_fraud:.4f}")
print(f"Posterior = {posterior_fraud:.2%}")

P(Alert) = 0.0585
P(Fraud | Alert) = 0.1538
Posterior = 15.38%

Read Bayes' theorem as a counting argument¶

[ P(F\mid A)¶

\frac{P(A\mid F)P(F)} {P(A)}. ]

Imagine 100,000 transactions.

  • About 1,000 are fraudulent.
  • About 900 of those trigger an alert.
  • About 99,000 are legitimate.
  • About 4,950 legitimate transactions also trigger alerts.

So the alert population contains many more false alerts than the sensitivity figure alone might suggest.

In [4]:
population_size = 100_000

expected_frauds = population_size * prior_fraud
expected_legitimate = population_size - expected_frauds

true_alerts = expected_frauds * sensitivity
false_alerts = expected_legitimate * false_positive_rate

bayes_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Group": ["Fraud", "Legitimate"],
    "Transactions": [expected_frauds, expected_legitimate],
    "Alerts": [true_alerts, false_alerts]
})

bayes_table
Out[4]:
Group Transactions Alerts
0 Fraud 1000.0 900.0
1 Legitimate 99000.0 4950.0
In [5]:
source = ColumnDataSource({
    "group": ["Fraud alerts", "Legitimate alerts"],
    "alerts": [true_alerts, false_alerts]
})

p = figure(
    x_range=["Fraud alerts", "Legitimate alerts"],
    width=760,
    height=380,
    title="Where Do Alerts Come From?"
)

p.vbar(x="group", top="alerts", width=0.55, source=source)
p.add_tools(HoverTool(tooltips=[("Group", "@group"), ("Alerts", "@alerts{0,0}")]))
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Expected alerts among 100,000 transactions"

show(p)

Interpretation¶

The detector has high sensitivity, yet the posterior probability of fraud after an alert is much smaller than 90%.

Why?

Because fraud is rare. The base rate matters.

This is an important lesson in:

  • fraud detection,
  • medical screening,
  • anomaly detection,
  • imbalanced classification,
  • rare-event monitoring.

Simulation check¶

The formula gives the theoretical answer. Now generate 500,000 transactions from the model and estimate the posterior empirically.

In [6]:
N = 500_000

is_fraud = RNG.random(N) < prior_fraud

alerts = np.where(
    is_fraud,
    RNG.random(N) < sensitivity,
    RNG.random(N) < false_positive_rate
)

empirical = is_fraud[alerts].mean()

print(f"Theoretical posterior: {posterior_fraud:.5f}")
print(f"Simulated posterior:   {empirical:.5f}")

Theoretical posterior: 0.15385
Simulated posterior:   0.15617

Scenario simulation — Vary the fraud base rate¶

Keep the detector unchanged.

Before running the next cell, predict what should happen to

[ P(F\mid A) ]

as fraud becomes more common.

In [7]:
priors = np.linspace(0.001, 0.20, 250)

posteriors = (
    sensitivity * priors
    /
    (
        sensitivity * priors
        + false_positive_rate * (1 - priors)
    )
)

p = figure(
    width=820,
    height=420,
    title="Posterior Probability vs Fraud Base Rate"
)

p.line(priors, posteriors, line_width=3)
p.xaxis.axis_label = "Prior P(Fraud)"
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Posterior P(Fraud | Alert)"

show(p)

Student checkpoint¶

Explain in one sentence why the curve rises.

Expected reasoning: when genuine fraud becomes more prevalent, a larger fraction of all alerts comes from true fraud rather than false positives.

Common mistake¶

[ P(F\mid A)=P(A\mid F) ]

is generally false. Always read the condition after the vertical bar as the information you already know.

Part B — Random variables and distributions¶

A random variable maps uncertain outcomes to numbers.

[ X:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb R ]

Examples:

  • number of failed servers,
  • waiting time until the next API request,
  • daily transaction count,
  • latency of a request.

Once we define (X), its uncertainty is described by a probability distribution.

2. PMF, PDF and CDF¶

Discrete variable¶

A probability mass function is

[ p_X(x)=P(X=x). ]

Continuous variable¶

A density satisfies

[ P(a<X<b)=\int_a^b f_X(x),dx. ]

For continuous (X),

[ P(X=x)=0. ]

CDF¶

For both types,

[ F_X(x)=P(X\le x). ]

Think of the CDF as an accumulating probability meter.

Case Study 2 — Data-centre reliability with the Binomial model¶

Suppose a platform operates 50 servers.

Each server independently has probability

[ p=0.04 ]

of failing during a day.

Let

[ X=\text{number of failed servers}. ]

Then

[ X\sim Binomial(50,0.04). ]

Assumptions¶

The Binomial model requires:

  1. fixed number of trials,
  2. two outcomes per trial,
  3. constant success/failure probability,
  4. independence.

A shared power outage, for example, would violate independence.

In [8]:
n_servers = 50
p_failure = 0.04

x = np.arange(n_servers + 1)

pmf = stats.binom.pmf(x, n_servers, p_failure)
cdf = stats.binom.cdf(x, n_servers, p_failure)

print("E[X]   =", n_servers * p_failure)
print("Var(X) =", n_servers * p_failure * (1 - p_failure))

E[X]   = 2.0
Var(X) = 1.92
In [9]:
p1 = figure(width=430, height=330, title="Binomial PMF")
p1.vbar(x=x, top=pmf, width=0.8)
p1.x_range.start = -0.5
p1.x_range.end = 12
p1.xaxis.axis_label = "Number of failures"
p1.yaxis.axis_label = "P(X=x)"

p2 = figure(width=430, height=330, title="Binomial CDF")
p2.step(x, cdf, mode="after", line_width=3)
p2.x_range.start = -0.5
p2.x_range.end = 12
p2.xaxis.axis_label = "x"
p2.yaxis.axis_label = "P(X≤x)"

show(row(p1, p2))

Practical questions¶

[ P(X=0) ]

means no server fails.

[ P(X\le2) ]

means at most two fail.

[ P(X\ge5) ]

can represent an unusually severe operational day.

In [10]:
print("P(no failures) =", stats.binom.pmf(0, n_servers, p_failure))
print("P(X <= 2)      =", stats.binom.cdf(2, n_servers, p_failure))
print("P(X >= 5)      =", stats.binom.sf(4, n_servers, p_failure))

P(no failures) = 0.1298857935220386
P(X <= 2)      = 0.6767140040965933
P(X >= 5)      = 0.04897147188451279

Simulation — What does a probability distribution mean operationally?¶

Imagine repeating the same day 100,000 times under identical assumptions.

The empirical frequency of each failure count should approach the theoretical PMF.

In [11]:
simulated_days = RNG.binomial(
    n_servers,
    p_failure,
    size=100_000
)

empirical_frequency = (
    pd.Series(simulated_days)
    .value_counts(normalize=True)
    .sort_index()
)

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "failures": np.arange(10),
    "theoretical": [
        stats.binom.pmf(k, n_servers, p_failure)
        for k in range(10)
    ],
    "empirical": [
        empirical_frequency.get(k, 0.0)
        for k in range(10)
    ]
})

comparison

Scenario simulation — Change (n) and (p)¶

Look for three things:

  1. Where is the distribution centered?
  2. How wide is it?
  3. Is it symmetric or skewed?

Before running, predict which scenario should look most symmetric.

In [13]:
scenarios = [
    (20, 0.05),
    (50, 0.10),
    (50, 0.50),
    (100, 0.80)
]

plots = []

for n_, p_ in scenarios:
    xs = np.arange(n_ + 1)
    probs = stats.binom.pmf(xs, n_, p_)

    fig = figure(
        width=400,
        height=300,
        title=f"Binomial(n={n_}, p={p_})"
    )

    fig.vbar(x=xs, top=probs, width=0.8)
    fig.xaxis.axis_label = "x"
    fig.yaxis.axis_label = "P(X=x)"
    plots.append(fig)

show(gridplot(plots, ncols=2))

3. Poisson distribution — counts of rare events¶

The Poisson PMF is

[ P(X=k)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}. ]

It is useful for counts such as:

  • incidents per hour,
  • requests per second,
  • defects per batch,
  • claims per day.

A distinctive property is

[ E[X]=Var(X)=\lambda. ]

Binomial-to-Poisson approximation¶

If

[ n\text{ is large},\qquad p\text{ is small}, ]

while

[ np=\lambda, ]

then

[ Binomial(n,p)\approx Poisson(\lambda). ]

In [14]:
lam = n_servers * p_failure
xs = np.arange(12)

binom_probs = stats.binom.pmf(xs, n_servers, p_failure)
poisson_probs = stats.poisson.pmf(xs, lam)

p = figure(
    width=820,
    height=400,
    title="Binomial vs Poisson Approximation"
)

p.line(xs, binom_probs, line_width=3, legend_label="Binomial")
p.scatter(xs, binom_probs, size=8)

p.line(
    xs,
    poisson_probs,
    line_width=3,
    line_dash="dashed",
    legend_label="Poisson"
)

p.scatter(xs, poisson_probs, size=8, marker="square")

p.xaxis.axis_label = "Number of failures"
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Probability"

show(p)

Scenario simulation — When does the Poisson approximation improve?¶

Keep (n=50) and change (p).

Predict whether (p=0.01) or (p=0.30) should give the closer approximation.

In [15]:
p_values = [0.30, 0.10, 0.04, 0.01]
plots = []

for p_ in p_values:
    lam_ = 50 * p_
    xmax = max(12, int(lam_ + 5 * np.sqrt(max(lam_, 1))))
    xs = np.arange(xmax + 1)

    b = stats.binom.pmf(xs, 50, p_)
    q = stats.poisson.pmf(xs, lam_)

    fig = figure(
        width=400,
        height=300,
        title=f"n=50, p={p_}, λ={lam_:.2f}"
    )

    fig.line(xs, b, line_width=2, legend_label="Binomial")
    fig.line(xs, q, line_width=2, line_dash="dashed", legend_label="Poisson")
    plots.append(fig)

show(gridplot(plots, ncols=2))

Case Study 3 — API traffic and Exponential waiting times¶

Suppose requests arrive at an average rate

[ \lambda=4 ]

per minute.

Under a homogeneous Poisson-process model, the waiting time until the next request is

[ T\sim Exponential(4). ]

The density is

[ f(t)=\lambda e^{-\lambda t},\qquad t\ge0. ]

Its mean is

[ E[T]=\frac1\lambda=0.25\text{ minutes}. ]

In [16]:
rate = 4.0

t = np.linspace(0, 2, 600)
pdf = stats.expon.pdf(t, scale=1/rate)
cdf = stats.expon.cdf(t, scale=1/rate)

p1 = figure(width=430, height=330, title="Exponential PDF")
p1.line(t, pdf, line_width=3)
p1.xaxis.axis_label = "Waiting time (minutes)"
p1.yaxis.axis_label = "Density"

p2 = figure(width=430, height=330, title="Exponential CDF")
p2.line(t, cdf, line_width=3)
p2.xaxis.axis_label = "Waiting time (minutes)"
p2.yaxis.axis_label = "P(T≤t)"

show(row(p1, p2))

Continuous probability interpretation¶

For a continuous variable,

[ P(T=0.5)=0. ]

The density height at (0.5) is not the probability of exactly 0.5.

Probabilities come from areas.

For example,

[ P(T>t)=e^{-\lambda t}. ]

In [17]:
for seconds in [5, 10, 20, 30, 60]:
    minutes = seconds / 60
    prob = stats.expon.sf(minutes, scale=1/rate)
    print(f"P(wait > {seconds:>2} sec) = {prob:.4f}")

P(wait >  5 sec) = 0.7165
P(wait > 10 sec) = 0.5134
P(wait > 20 sec) = 0.2636
P(wait > 30 sec) = 0.1353
P(wait > 60 sec) = 0.0183

Scenario simulation — Change traffic intensity¶

Since

[ E[T]=\frac1\lambda, ]

doubling the arrival rate should halve the expected waiting time.

Look at how the distribution compresses toward zero as (\lambda) increases.

In [18]:
rates = [1, 2, 4, 8]

p = figure(
    width=820,
    height=420,
    title="Exponential Waiting Times at Different Arrival Rates"
)

t = np.linspace(0, 3, 600)

for r_ in rates:
    p.line(
        t,
        stats.expon.pdf(t, scale=1/r_),
        line_width=2,
        legend_label=f"λ={r_}"
    )

p.xaxis.axis_label = "Waiting time"
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Density"

show(p)

4. Expectation, variance and dependence¶

Expectation describes long-run centre.

For discrete (X),

[ E[X]=\sum_x xP(X=x). ]

Variance measures squared spread around the mean:

[ Var(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2] ]

and equivalently

[ Var(X)=E[X^2]-E[X]^2. ]

Standard deviation is

[ SD(X)=\sqrt{Var(X)}. ]

In [19]:
# Biased die example
values = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
probs = np.array([0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.20, 0.30])

theoretical_mean = np.sum(values * probs)
theoretical_var = np.sum(values**2 * probs) - theoretical_mean**2

draws = RNG.choice(values, size=300_000, p=probs)

print("Theoretical mean:", theoretical_mean)
print("Empirical mean:  ", draws.mean())
print("Theoretical var: ", theoretical_var)
print("Empirical var:   ", draws.var())

Theoretical mean: 4.3
Empirical mean:   4.299663333333333
Theoretical var:  2.3099999999999987
Empirical var:    2.3149518866555554

Same mean, different uncertainty¶

Two systems can have the same average latency but very different stability.

That is why a mean alone is often not enough.

In [20]:
system_a = RNG.normal(100, 8, 30_000)
system_b = RNG.normal(100, 35, 30_000)

hist_a, edges_a = np.histogram(system_a, bins=60, density=True)
hist_b, edges_b = np.histogram(system_b, bins=60, density=True)

centers_a = (edges_a[:-1] + edges_a[1:]) / 2
centers_b = (edges_b[:-1] + edges_b[1:]) / 2

p = figure(width=820, height=420, title="Same Mean, Different Variability")
p.line(centers_a, hist_a, line_width=3, legend_label="System A")
p.line(centers_b, hist_b, line_width=3, legend_label="System B")
p.xaxis.axis_label = "Latency"
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Density"

show(p)

Covariance and correlation¶

For two random variables,

[ Cov(X,Y)¶

E[(X-E[X])(Y-E[Y])] ]

and

[ Corr(X,Y)¶

\frac{Cov(X,Y)} {\sigma_X\sigma_Y}. ]

Correlation measures linear association, not arbitrary dependence.

In [21]:
def correlated_sample(rho, n=2500):
    covariance = np.array([[1, rho], [rho, 1]])
    sample = RNG.multivariate_normal([0, 0], covariance, size=n)
    return sample[:, 0], sample[:, 1]

rhos = [-0.85, 0.0, 0.45, 0.90]
plots = []

for rho in rhos:
    x_, y_ = correlated_sample(rho)
    observed = np.corrcoef(x_, y_)[0, 1]

    fig = figure(
        width=390,
        height=300,
        title=f"Observed corr ≈ {observed:.2f}"
    )
    fig.scatter(x_, y_, size=4, alpha=0.25)
    fig.xaxis.axis_label = "X"
    fig.yaxis.axis_label = "Y"
    plots.append(fig)

show(gridplot(plots, ncols=2))

Important counterexample¶

Let

[ Y=X^2 ]

with symmetric (X).

Then (Y) is completely determined by (X), so they are dependent. Yet their linear correlation can be near zero.

In [22]:
x_dep = RNG.uniform(-1, 1, 4000)
y_dep = x_dep**2
corr = np.corrcoef(x_dep, y_dep)[0, 1]

p = figure(
    width=760,
    height=420,
    title=f"Dependent but Nearly Uncorrelated (corr={corr:.4f})"
)
p.scatter(x_dep, y_dep, size=4, alpha=0.25)
p.xaxis.axis_label = "X"
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Y=X²"

show(p)

Part C — Sampling distributions¶

Now we move from one random observation to an entire random sample.

Suppose

[ X_1,\ldots,X_n ]

are IID with

[ E[X_i]=\mu,\qquad Var(X_i)=\sigma^2. ]

The sample mean is

[ \bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i. ]

Because a different sample gives a different mean, (\bar X) is itself random.

Its distribution across repeated samples is the sampling distribution.

Case Study 4 — Central Limit Theorem with skewed latency¶

Raw response times are often strongly right-skewed.

We deliberately generate a log-normal latency population.

The Central Limit Theorem tells us that the distribution of the sample mean, after suitable standardisation, approaches Normality as (n) increases.

It does not say the raw latency becomes Normal.

In [23]:
population = RNG.lognormal(
    mean=4.2,
    sigma=0.8,
    size=400_000
)

hist, edges = np.histogram(population, bins=80, density=True)
centers = (edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2

p = figure(
    width=820,
    height=420,
    title="Raw Latency Population: Strong Right Skew"
)
p.line(centers, hist, line_width=3)
p.x_range.end = np.quantile(population, 0.995)
p.xaxis.axis_label = "Latency"
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Density"

show(p)

Central Limit Theorem¶

Under broad conditions,

[ \frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \overset{d}{\longrightarrow} N(0,1). ]

Three things happen as (n) grows:

  1. the sampling distribution becomes more bell-shaped,
  2. its center stays near (\mu),
  3. it becomes narrower.
In [24]:
def simulate_sample_means(sample_size, repetitions=15_000):
    samples = RNG.lognormal(
        mean=4.2,
        sigma=0.8,
        size=(repetitions, sample_size)
    )
    return samples.mean(axis=1)

sample_sizes = [1, 5, 30, 100]
plots = []

for n_ in sample_sizes:
    means = simulate_sample_means(n_)
    hist, edges = np.histogram(means, bins=60, density=True)
    centers = (edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2

    fig = figure(
        width=400,
        height=300,
        title=f"Sampling distribution of mean, n={n_}"
    )
    fig.line(centers, hist, line_width=3)
    fig.xaxis.axis_label = "Sample mean"
    fig.yaxis.axis_label = "Density"
    plots.append(fig)

show(gridplot(plots, ncols=2))

Standard error¶

The sample mean satisfies

[ E[\bar X]=\mu ]

and

[ Var(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}. ]

Therefore

[ SE(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}. ]

This is the spread of sample means, not the spread of individual observations.

In [25]:
large_population = RNG.lognormal(mean=4.2, sigma=0.8, size=1_000_000)
sigma_pop = large_population.std(ddof=0)

rows = []

for n_ in [5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200]:
    means = RNG.choice(
        large_population,
        size=(5000, n_),
        replace=True
    ).mean(axis=1)

    rows.append({
        "n": n_,
        "empirical_se": means.std(ddof=1),
        "theoretical_se": sigma_pop / np.sqrt(n_)
    })

se_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
se_df

Important efficiency consequence¶

To cut standard error in half, you need roughly four times as much data:

[ \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{4n}}¶

\frac12\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}. ]

More data helps, but precision improves only at a square-root rate.

Scenario simulation — CLT under different population shapes¶

We compare sample means from:

  • Uniform,
  • Exponential,
  • Log-normal,
  • Bimodal populations.

Use (n=40) in every case.

The point is not that every case is perfectly Normal by 40. The point is to see how averaging changes shape across very different populations.

In [27]:
def draw_population(kind, size):
    if kind == "Uniform":
        return RNG.uniform(0, 1, size)
    if kind == "Exponential":
        return RNG.exponential(1, size)
    if kind == "Lognormal":
        return RNG.lognormal(0, 0.8, size)
    if kind == "Bimodal":
        selector = RNG.random(size) < 0.5
        return np.where(
            selector,
            RNG.normal(-2, 0.6, size),
            RNG.normal(2, 0.6, size)
        )
    raise ValueError(kind)

kinds = ["Uniform", "Exponential", "Lognormal", "Bimodal"]
plots = []

for kind in kinds:
    reps = 8000
    n_ = 40

    data = draw_population(kind, reps * n_).reshape(reps, n_)
    means = data.mean(axis=1)

    hist, edges = np.histogram(means, bins=55, density=True)
    centers = (edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2

    fig = figure(
        width=400,
        height=300,
        title=f"{kind}: sample means, n={n_}"
    )
    fig.line(centers, hist, line_width=3)
    plots.append(fig)

show(gridplot(plots, ncols=2))

Part D — Statistical inference¶

Statistics asks:

[ \boxed{\text{observed sample} \rightarrow \text{unknown population parameter}} ]

Examples of parameters include

[ \mu,\qquad p,\qquad \sigma^2. ]

A statistic such as

[ \bar X ]

is random before sampling and becomes an observed number after data are collected.

5. Point estimation and confidence intervals¶

A point estimator gives one number:

[ \hat\mu=\bar X. ]

But a single estimate hides sampling uncertainty.

A confidence interval adds a margin of error:

[ \boxed{\text{estimate} \pm \text{uncertainty}}. ]

For a Normal population with unknown (\sigma),

[ T= \frac{\bar X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n} \sim t_{n-1}. ]

So a (100(1-\alpha)%) confidence interval is

[ \bar X \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{S}{\sqrt n}. ]

In [28]:
x = np.linspace(-4.5, 4.5, 800)

p = figure(
    width=820,
    height=420,
    title="Student's t Approaches the Normal Distribution"
)

p.line(x, stats.norm.pdf(x), line_width=3, legend_label="Normal")

for df in [2, 5, 10, 30]:
    p.line(
        x,
        stats.t.pdf(x, df),
        line_width=2,
        legend_label=f"t(df={df})"
    )

p.xaxis.axis_label = "x"
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Density"

show(p)

Why does the t distribution have heavier tails?¶

When (\sigma) is unknown, we estimate it using (S).

That extra uncertainty makes extreme standardized values somewhat more plausible than under a standard Normal model.

As sample size increases, (S) becomes more stable and the t distribution approaches Normality.

Case Study 5 — Repeated confidence intervals¶

Suppose the true population is

[ X\sim N(50,8^2). ]

We repeatedly:

  1. sample (n=25) observations,
  2. compute a 95% t-confidence interval,
  3. check whether it covers the true (\mu=50).

The correct frequentist interpretation is about the long-run procedure.

In [29]:
true_mu = 50
true_sigma = 8
sample_size = 25
experiments = 100
confidence_level = 0.95

alpha = 1 - confidence_level
records = []

for i in range(experiments):
    sample = RNG.normal(true_mu, true_sigma, sample_size)

    xbar = sample.mean()
    s = sample.std(ddof=1)

    critical = stats.t.ppf(
        1 - alpha / 2,
        df=sample_size - 1
    )

    margin = critical * s / np.sqrt(sample_size)

    lower = xbar - margin
    upper = xbar + margin

    records.append({
        "experiment": i,
        "mean": xbar,
        "lower": lower,
        "upper": upper,
        "covers": lower <= true_mu <= upper
    })

ci_df = pd.DataFrame(records)

print("Observed coverage:", ci_df["covers"].mean())

Observed coverage: 0.94
In [30]:
p = figure(
    width=900,
    height=680,
    title="Repeated 95% Confidence Intervals"
)

for _, r in ci_df.iterrows():
    p.line(
        [r["lower"], r["upper"]],
        [r["experiment"], r["experiment"]],
        line_width=2,
        alpha=0.75
    )
    p.scatter([r["mean"]], [r["experiment"]], size=5)

p.add_layout(
    Span(
        location=true_mu,
        dimension="height",
        line_dash="dashed",
        line_width=3
    )
)

p.xaxis.axis_label = "Mean estimate / interval"
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Repeated sample"

show(p)

Student checkpoint¶

Some intervals miss the true mean. That is expected.

A 95% confidence procedure should cover the fixed parameter about 95% of the time over repeated sampling.

Do not interpret the observed 95% interval as a Bayesian 95% posterior probability statement.

Scenario simulation — Confidence level, sample size and interval width¶

Approximate width for a mean is proportional to

[ \text{critical value} \times \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}. ]

Therefore:

  • larger (n) → narrower interval,
  • larger variability → wider interval,
  • higher confidence → wider interval.

Higher confidence costs precision.

In [31]:
sample_sizes = [10, 20, 50, 100, 200]
levels = [0.90, 0.95, 0.99]
sigma = 10

rows = []

for level in levels:
    alpha = 1 - level

    for n_ in sample_sizes:
        critical = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2)
        width = 2 * critical * sigma / np.sqrt(n_)

        rows.append({
            "n": n_,
            "level": f"{int(level*100)}%",
            "width": width
        })

width_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)

p = figure(
    width=820,
    height=420,
    title="Confidence Interval Width vs Sample Size"
)

for level in width_df["level"].unique():
    subset = width_df[width_df["level"] == level]

    p.line(
        subset["n"],
        subset["width"],
        line_width=3,
        legend_label=level
    )
    p.scatter(subset["n"], subset["width"], size=7)

p.xaxis.axis_label = "Sample size"
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Approximate interval width"

show(p)

6. Hypothesis testing¶

A hypothesis test asks:

If the null hypothesis were true, how surprising would the observed statistic be?

For a one-sample mean,

[ H_0:\mu=\mu_0 ]

and perhaps

[ H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0. ]

With unknown variance,

[ T= \frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt n}. ]

The p-value is a tail probability computed under (H_0).

It is not

[ P(H_0\mid data). ]

In [32]:
xx = np.linspace(-4, 4, 1000)
yy = stats.norm.pdf(xx)

critical = stats.norm.ppf(0.975)

p = figure(
    width=820,
    height=420,
    title="Two-Sided Rejection Regions at α=0.05"
)

p.line(xx, yy, line_width=3)

left = xx <= -critical
right = xx >= critical

p.varea(x=xx[left], y1=0, y2=yy[left], alpha=0.35)
p.varea(x=xx[right], y1=0, y2=yy[right], alpha=0.35)

p.add_layout(Span(location=-critical, dimension="height", line_dash="dashed"))
p.add_layout(Span(location=critical, dimension="height", line_dash="dashed"))

p.xaxis.axis_label = "Test statistic"
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Density"

show(p)

Type I, Type II errors and power¶

Reality Fail to reject (H_0) Reject (H_0)
(H_0) true Correct Type I error
(H_0) false Type II error Correct

[ \alpha=P(\text{Type I error}) ]

[ \beta=P(\text{Type II error}) ]

[ Power=1-\beta. ]

Power answers:

If a real effect exists, how likely is my experiment to detect it?

Case Study 6 — A/B testing conversion rates¶

Suppose:

[ p_A=0.08 ]

and Variant B may improve conversion to

[ p_B=0.095. ]

We test

[ H_0:p_A=p_B ]

against

[ H_1:p_A\ne p_B. ]

This single case study connects Bernoulli variables, Binomial counts, normal approximations, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and power.

In [33]:
n_A = 5000
n_B = 5000

true_p_A = 0.080
true_p_B = 0.095

A = RNG.binomial(1, true_p_A, n_A)
B = RNG.binomial(1, true_p_B, n_B)

pA_hat = A.mean()
pB_hat = B.mean()

print(f"A conversion = {pA_hat:.3%}")
print(f"B conversion = {pB_hat:.3%}")
print(f"Observed lift = {(pB_hat-pA_hat):.3%}")

A conversion = 7.620%
B conversion = 8.960%
Observed lift = 1.340%

Two-proportion z-test¶

Under the null hypothesis, use the pooled rate

[ \hat p= \frac{x_A+x_B}{n_A+n_B}. ]

Then

[ SE_0= \sqrt{ \hat p(1-\hat p) \left( \frac1{n_A}+\frac1{n_B} \right) } ]

and

[ Z= \frac{\hat p_B-\hat p_A}{SE_0}. ]

In [34]:
x_A = A.sum()
x_B = B.sum()

pooled = (x_A + x_B) / (n_A + n_B)

se0 = np.sqrt(
    pooled * (1 - pooled)
    * (1/n_A + 1/n_B)
)

z = (pB_hat - pA_hat) / se0
p_value = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z))

print(f"z statistic = {z:.4f}")
print(f"p-value     = {p_value:.6f}")

z statistic = 2.4299
p-value     = 0.015103

Confidence interval for the conversion difference¶

For estimation, use the unpooled standard error

[ SE= \sqrt{ \frac{\hat p_A(1-\hat p_A)}{n_A} + \frac{\hat p_B(1-\hat p_B)}{n_B} }. ]

Then construct an interval for

[ p_B-p_A. ]

This answers a richer question than "significant or not":

What range of effect sizes is compatible with the data?

In [35]:
diff = pB_hat - pA_hat

se_diff = np.sqrt(
    pA_hat * (1 - pA_hat) / n_A
    + pB_hat * (1 - pB_hat) / n_B
)

critical = stats.norm.ppf(0.975)

ci_low = diff - critical * se_diff
ci_high = diff + critical * se_diff

print(f"Estimated difference = {diff:.4%}")
print(f"95% CI = ({ci_low:.4%}, {ci_high:.4%})")

Estimated difference = 1.3400%
95% CI = (0.2595%, 2.4205%)
In [36]:
groups = ["A", "B"]
rates = [pA_hat, pB_hat]

p = figure(
    x_range=groups,
    width=700,
    height=380,
    title="Observed Conversion Rates"
)

p.vbar(x=groups, top=rates, width=0.55)
p.y_range.start = 0
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Conversion rate"

show(p)

7. Statistical power through simulation¶

Power is easiest to understand by repeating the entire experiment many times.

For a chosen sample size:

  1. simulate Variant A,
  2. simulate Variant B,
  3. run a two-proportion z-test,
  4. record whether (p<0.05),
  5. repeat many times.

If the alternative is truly correct, the fraction of rejections estimates power.

In [37]:
def two_prop_z_test(x_a, n_a, x_b, n_b):
    p_a = x_a / n_a
    p_b = x_b / n_b

    pooled = (x_a + x_b) / (n_a + n_b)

    se = np.sqrt(
        pooled * (1 - pooled)
        * (1/n_a + 1/n_b)
    )

    if se == 0:
        return 0.0, 1.0

    z = (p_b - p_a) / se
    p_value = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z))

    return z, p_value


def estimate_power(
    n,
    p_a=0.08,
    p_b=0.095,
    repetitions=2000,
    alpha=0.05
):
    rejections = 0

    for _ in range(repetitions):
        x_a = RNG.binomial(n, p_a)
        x_b = RNG.binomial(n, p_b)

        _, p_value = two_prop_z_test(
            x_a, n, x_b, n
        )

        rejections += p_value < alpha

    return rejections / repetitions
In [38]:
sample_sizes = [200, 400, 800, 1200, 2000, 3000, 5000, 8000]

powers = [
    estimate_power(n)
    for n in sample_sizes
]

power_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "n_per_group": sample_sizes,
    "estimated_power": powers

Scenario simulation — Effect size versus power¶

Keep sample size fixed and vary the true B conversion probability.

Before running:

Which is easier to detect: a 0.2 percentage-point improvement or a 2.5 percentage-point improvement?

A larger effect should separate the null and alternative sampling distributions more strongly.

Interpretation¶

Power generally increases when:

  • sample size increases,
  • true effect size increases,
  • measurement noise decreases,
  • the significance threshold becomes less strict.

This is why experimental design should be planned before data collection rather than after seeing the p-value.

Case Study 7 — Paired inference for system optimisation¶

Suppose we benchmark the same 60 API endpoints before and after an optimisation.

Because endpoint (i) before optimisation corresponds directly to endpoint (i) after optimisation, the data are paired.

Define

[ D_i¶

X_{i,\text{before}}¶

X_{i,\text{after}}. ]

Then test

[ H_0:\mu_D=0. ]

This becomes a one-sample t-test on the differences.

In [42]:
n_endpoints = 60

endpoint_baseline = RNG.normal(180, 30, n_endpoints)

before = (
    endpoint_baseline
    + RNG.normal(0, 12, n_endpoints)
)

after = (
    endpoint_baseline
    - 12
    + RNG.normal(0, 12, n_endpoints)
)

differences = before - after

t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_1samp(
    differences,
    popmean=0
)

mean_diff = differences.mean()
se_diff = stats.sem(differences)

critical = stats.t.ppf(
    0.975,
    df=n_endpoints - 1
)

ci = (
    mean_diff - critical * se_diff,
    mean_diff + critical * se_diff
)

print(f"Average improvement = {mean_diff:.3f} ms")
print(f"t statistic         = {t_stat:.3f}")
print(f"p-value             = {p_value:.6f}")
print(f"95% CI              = ({ci[0]:.3f}, {ci[1]:.3f})")

Average improvement = 11.838 ms
t statistic         = 5.590
p-value             = 0.000001
95% CI              = (7.601, 16.075)

idx = np.arange(n_endpoints)

p = figure(
    width=860,
    height=420,
    title="Same Endpoints Before and After Optimisation"
)

p.scatter(
    idx,
    before,
    size=6,
    alpha=0.7,
    legend_label="Before"
)

p.scatter(
    idx,
    after,
    size=6,
    alpha=0.7,
    marker="square",
    legend_label="After"

p.xaxis.axis_label = "Endpoint"
p.yaxis.axis_label = "Latency (ms)"

show(p)

Why pairing helps¶

Different endpoints naturally have different baseline latencies.

If we compare raw before/after groups independently, that endpoint-to-endpoint variability contributes noise.

With paired differences, much of the stable endpoint-specific baseline cancels.

Pairing is useful when observations have a meaningful one-to-one relationship.

8. Chi-square and F distributions¶

For Normal observations,

[ \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-1}. ]

This enables inference about population variance.

Ratios of appropriately scaled independent variance estimates lead to the F distribution.

These distributions are usually right-skewed for small degrees of freedom and become more concentrated as degrees of freedom increase.

In [45]:
x_chi = np.linspace(0.001, 25, 700)
x_f = np.linspace(0.001, 5, 700)

p1 = figure(width=430, height=330, title="Chi-square Distributions")

for df in [1, 3, 5, 10]:
    p1.line(
        x_chi,
        stats.chi2.pdf(x_chi, df),
        line_width=2,
        legend_label=f"df={df}"
    )

p2 = figure(width=430, height=330, title="F Distributions")

for d1, d2 in [(2, 10), (5, 10), (10, 20)]:
    p2.line(
        x_f,
        stats.f.pdf(x_f, d1, d2),
        line_width=2,
        legend_label=f"F({d1},{d2})"
    )

show(row(p1, p2))

9. Common conceptual traps¶

These are worth revisiting after the simulations.

Trap 1 — Reverse conditional probability¶

[ P(A\mid B)\neq P(B\mid A) ]

in general.

Trap 2 — Density height equals probability¶

False for continuous random variables. Probability is area under the density.

Trap 3 — Zero correlation implies independence¶

False in general. Correlation only measures linear association.

Trap 4 — CLT says the raw data become Normal¶

False. The CLT concerns the sampling distribution of suitably standardized sums or means.

Trap 5 — A 95% confidence interval gives a 95% posterior probability for the fixed parameter¶

Not under the usual frequentist interpretation.

Trap 6 — A p-value is the probability that (H_0) is true¶

False. It is computed assuming (H_0) is true.

Trap 7 — Statistical significance implies practical importance¶

False. With huge samples, tiny effects can be statistically detectable but operationally irrelevant.

10. Guided scenario exercises¶

For every exercise, use this method:

  1. Define the random variable.
  2. State the model/distribution.
  3. List assumptions.
  4. Calculate analytically if possible.
  5. Simulate the scenario.
  6. Visualize with Bokeh.
  7. Interpret in plain language.

Exercise A — Fraud prevalence¶

Keep:

[ P(A\mid F)=0.90, \qquad P(A\mid F^c)=0.05. ]

Compare priors

[ 0.001,;0.01,;0.05,;0.20. ]

Explain why the same detector produces different posterior probabilities in different populations.

Exercise B — Device failures¶

Suppose 200 devices independently fail with probability (0.01).

Compute:

[ E[X], \qquad P(X\ge5). ]

Then compare the exact Binomial probability with a Poisson approximation.

Exercise C — CLT stress test¶

Generate Exponential observations and compare sample means for

[ n=2,;10,;50,;500. ]

Do not assume there is a universal rule such as "(n=30) is always enough."

Exercise D — Confidence versus precision¶

Set

[ \sigma=20. ]

Compare interval widths for confidence levels 90%, 95%, 99% and sample sizes

[ 25,;100,;400. ]

Explain why more confidence creates a wider interval.

Exercise E — A/B test power¶

Keep (n=3000) per group and baseline conversion (0.08).

Compare Variant B probabilities

[ 0.081,;0.085,;0.090,;0.100. ]

Estimate power by simulation and explain why tiny improvements are difficult to detect.

12. ST2334 concept map¶

The module can be understood as one connected chain:

[ \boxed{\text{Sample spaces and events}} ]

[ \downarrow ]

[ \boxed{\text{Conditional probability and Bayes}} ]

[ \downarrow ]

[ \boxed{\text{Random variables}} ]

[ \downarrow ]

[ \boxed{\text{PMF / PDF / CDF}} ]

[ \downarrow ]

[ \boxed{\text{Expectation, variance and dependence}} ]

[ \downarrow ]

[ \boxed{\text{Random samples}} ]

[ \downarrow ]

[ \boxed{\text{Sampling distributions}} ]

[ \downarrow ]

[ \boxed{\text{CLT and standard error}} ]

[ \downarrow ]

[ \boxed{\text{Point and interval estimation}} ]

[ \downarrow ]

[ \boxed{\text{Hypothesis testing}} ]

[ \downarrow ]

[ \boxed{\text{Type I/II errors and power}} ]

The deepest transition is:

[ \boxed{ \text{Probability: model}\rightarrow\text{data} } ]

versus

[ \boxed{ \text{Statistics: data}\rightarrow\text{unknown model parameter} } ]

13. Recommended study workflow¶

First pass¶

Run every cell and focus on intuition.

Second pass¶

Before every scenario plot, predict what the graph should do.

Third pass¶

Change one parameter at a time:

  • prior probability,
  • (n),
  • (p),
  • (\lambda),
  • population skew,
  • confidence level,
  • effect size.

Fourth pass¶

Reproduce each derivation without looking.

Fifth pass¶

Explain each case study verbally to another student.

If you can explain why a simulation behaves as it does, you understand the material more deeply than if you only remember the corresponding formula.
